In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the second-order adiabadic perturbation theory is a very useful tool for calculating the quasi-energies of atoms and molecules in low-frequency ac-fields.

the perturbative approach presented here is an efficient method for the calculations of energy shifts (positions), widths, and transition amplitudes for atoms and molecules interacting with low-frequency ac-electric fields.
the perturbation theory presented here is a promising method to obtain the quasienergy spectrum for atoms and molecules exposed to low-frequency ac fields.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we present a new method for calculating the Floquet solutions in the low-frequency, ω, regime and we show the feasibility of the method for calculating the energy shifts and the energy widths in the low-frequency ω regime.

the perturbation theory approach presented here is a viable and practical approach for the calculations in the low-frequency, ω, regime and it can be used for the calculations of atomic, molecular and nuclear energy shifts (positions), widths (inverse lifeties), and quasi-energy spectrum.

we have developed a perturbation scheme that allows the calculation of energy positions and widths for atoms and molecules exposed to low-frequency laser fields at the same level as the calculations of the dc-field effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the perturbative approach presented in this work can be used to calculate the Floquet solutions for the ac-fields in the low-frequency, ω, regime using the same level of accuracy as the calculations of the dc-field induced energy shifts and widths using the standard electronic structure methods.

the perturbative approach presented here can be used to obtain the quasi-energy spectrum and its associated Floquet states of atoms and molecules exposed to low-frequency ac-fields, which are in the range of the atomic/molecular energy scale.
in the low-frequency, ω, regime, the quasienergy spectrum can be obtained by a perturbation approach, which is based on the adiabatically dressed Hamiltonian.
